texts.facts: This appeal arises out of the award passed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Attingal dated 27.3.2013 in O.P.(MV) No.1007 of 2008, an application filed under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 claiming compensation on account of the death of one Ajayakumar, the husband of the appellant/first claimant and son of the fourth respondent/second claimant, who died in a motor accident occurred on 18.8.2008 while he was riding a motorcycle bearing Reg.No.KL-16/5643. At the place of accident, the motorcycle was hit by a KSRTC bus bearing Reg.No.KL-15/7027 owned and driven by respondents 1 and 2 respectively and insured with the third respondent. As a result of the accident, the deceased sustained fatal injuries, who succumbed to the injuries on the date of the accident itself. Alleging that the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the KSRTC bus by the second respondent driver, claim petition was filed before the Tribunal claiming a total compensation of Rs.27,00,000/- under different heads. 2. Before the Tribunal, the third respondent insurer filed written statement contending that the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent riding of the motorcycle by the deceased and not on account of any negligence on the part of the second respondent driver of the bus. The insurer has also raised a contention that the amount of compensation claimed is highly excessive. 3. Before the Tribunal, Exts.A1 to A15 were marked on the side of the claimants. Both sides have not chosen to adduce any oral evidence. Since the KSRTC bus was covered by a valid Bindhu Kumary vs Unknown on 27 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129775860/ 2 insurance policy, the third respondent insurer was directed to deposit the said amount before the Tribunal, together with interest at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of the petition till expiry of a period of 60 days from the date of award and thereafter, at the rate of 12% per annum, with proportionate cost. Out of the amount of compensation awarded, the appellant/first claimant was found entitled for a sum of Rs.8,00,000/- and the fourth respondent/second claimant a sum of Rs.2,89,265/-. 5. Dissatisfied with the quantum of compensation awarded by the Tribunal under different heads, the appellant/first claimant is before this Court in this appeal, arraying the second claimant as the fourth respondent. The appellant has also challenged the finding of the Tribunal regarding contributory negligence on the part of the deceased.
texts.arguments: 7. The learned counsel for the appellant would contend that the finding of the Tribunal regarding contributory on the part of the deceased cannot be sustained, since, as evident from the materials on record, the accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving of the KSRTC bus by the second respondent driver. The learned counsel would also contend that the compensation awarded by the Tribunal under different heads are grossly inadequate and the same requires enhancement in this appeal. 8. Per contra, the learned counsel for the third respondent insurer would contend that the finding of the Tribunal regarding contributory negligence on the part of the deceased is perfectly legal and supported by the materials on record, which warrants no interference in this appeal. The learned counsel would also contend that the compensation awarded by the Tribunal under different heads represents just and reasonable compensation, which requires no enhancement in this appeal. 10. In Sheji v. Muhammedali Shehabudeen and another (2016 (2) KHC 410) a Division Bench of this Court, in which one among us (Anil K. Narendran, J.) was a member, held that to prove contributory negligence, there must be cogent evidence. The Division Bench held further that, in a motor accident claim the claimants are merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability and that, standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt could not have been applied. Paras.12 and 13 of the said judgment read thus; "12. In Meera Devi v. H. P. Road Transport Corporation [(2014) 4 SCC 511] a Three-Judge Bench of the Apex Court reiterated that to prove contributory negligence, there must be cogent evidence. In the absence of any cogent and convincing, Bindhu Kumary vs Unknown on 27 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129775860/ 3 no contributory negligence can be attributed on the 1st respondent. 13. In Parameshwari v. Amir Chand [(2011) 11 SCC 635] the Apex Court held that, in a road accident claim, the strict principles of proof in a criminal case are not attracted. In the said judgment, the Apex Court had taken note of the observation made in its earlier judgment in Bimla Devi v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation [(2009) 13 SCC 530] that, the claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability and that standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt could not have been applied." 11. In Pramodkumar v. Karmasey Kunvargi Tak [(2002) 6 SCC 455] the Apex Court explained the distinction between 'negligence' and 'contributory negligence' by holding that, the question of contributory negligence arises when there has been some act or omission on the claimant's part, which has materially contributed to the damage caused, and is of such a nature that it may properly be described as 'negligence'. 'Negligence' ordinarily means breach of a legal duty to care, but when used in the expression 'contributory negligence' it does not mean breach of any duty. It only means the failure by a person to use reasonable care for the safety of either himself or his property, so that he becomes blameworthy in part as an 'author of his own wrong'. 12. In Pramodkumar's case (supra) the Apex Court held further that, subject to non requirement of the existence of duty, the question of contributory negligence is to be decided on the same principle on which the question of defendant's negligence is decided. The standard of a reasonable man is as relevant in the case of a plaintiff's contributory negligence as in the case of defendant's negligence. But the degree of want of care which will constitute contributory negligence, varies with the circumstances and the factual situation of the case. Where, by his negligence, if one party places another in a situation of danger, which compels the other to act quickly in order to extricate himself, it does not amount to contributory negligence if that other acts in a way, which, with the benefit of hindsight, is shown not to have been the best way out of the difficulty. Paras.9 and 10 of the said judgment read thus; "9. Subject to non-requirement of the existence of duty, the question of contributory negligence is to be decided on the same principle on which the question of defendant's negligence is decided. The following observation of the High Court of Australia in Astley v. Austrust Ltd. [(1999) 73 ALJR 403] is worthy of quoting; "A finding of contributory negligence turns on a factual investigation whether the plaintiff contributed to his or her own loss by failing to take reasonable care of his or her person or property. Bindhu Kumary vs Unknown on 27 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129775860/ 4 What is reasonable care depends on the circumstances of the case. In many cases, it may be proper for a plaintiff to rely on the defendant to perform its duty. But there is no absolute rule. The duties and responsibilities of the defendant are a variable factor in determining whether contributory negligence exists and, if so, to what degree. In some cases, the nature of the duty owed may exculpate the plaintiff from a claim of contributory negligence; in other cases, the nature of the duty may reduce the plaintiff's share of responsibility for the damage suffered; and in yet other cases the nature of the duty may not prevent a finding that the plaintiff failed to take reasonable care for the safety of his or her person or property. Contributory negligence focuses on the conduct of the plaintiff. The duty owed by the defendant, although relevant, is one only of many factors that must be weighed in determining whether the plaintiff has so conducted itself that it failed to take reasonable care for the safety of its person or property." 10. It has been accepted as a valid principle by various judicial authorities that where, by his negligence, if one party places another in a situation of danger, which compels that other to act quickly in order to extricate himself, it does not amount to contributory negligence if that other acts in a way, which, with the benefit of hindsight, is shown not to have been the best way out of the difficulty. In Swadling v. Cooper [1931 AC 1] AC at p.9 Lord Hailsham said: (All ER p.260 D-E) "Mere failure to avoid the collision by taking some extraordinary precaution does not in itself constituted negligence. The plaintiff has no right to complain if in the agony of the collision the defendant fails to take some step which might have prevented a collision unless that step is one which a reasonably careful man would fairly be expected to take in the circumstances." 13. In Jestine K.J. v. Prasad K. and others (2013 (4) KLT 916) a learned Judge of this Court held that, if the offending vehicle was driven in such a way that it put another person in sudden danger and he is thereby perplexed or agitated, he cannot be expected to exercise due care. If in that perplexed or agitated state of mind he does something or omits to do something which normally he is expected to do or not to do and consequently he suffers injury, he is entitled to claim and get compensation. Para.13 of the said judgment reads thus; "13. In London Steamboat Company v. Bywell Castle (1878 (9) Probate Division 219) it was held that where one ship has by wrong manoeuvres placed another ship in a position of extreme danger, that other ship will not be held to blame if she has done something wrong, and has not been manoeuvred with perfect skill and presence of mind. This rule has since then been known as the 'Bywell Castle Rule'. It means that where a person is put in sudden danger, he cannot be expected to exercise the due care, skill, coolness and wisdom which a man of ordinary prudence would have taken. The person or the plaintiff is perplexed or agitated by the act of the defendant. What is done or omitted to be done in the agony of the moment cannot fairly be treated as negligence [See also Jang Bahadur Singh v. Bindhu Kumary vs Unknown on 27 March, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129775860/ 5 14. Thus, if the intervention of the KSRTC bus driven by the second respondent driver at an exorbitant speed was such that it put the deceased who was riding the motorcycle in fear of sudden danger and the deceased in a perplexed or agitated mood and due to its agony did or omitted to do something, then, he cannot be said to be negligent. Since the deceased was aged 36 years, going by the decision of the Apex Court in Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation [2010 (2) KLT 802], the proper multiplier applicable is '15'. In Rajesh v. Rajbir Singh [2013 (3) KLT 89], the Apex Court awarded a sum of Rs.25,000/- as compensation under this head. In the instant case, the accident is of the year 2008. Though the deceased succumbed to the injuries on the date of accident itself, following the law laid down by a Division Bench of this Court in Jyni and others v. Raphel P.T and others [ILR 2016 (2) Kerala 54], we deem it appropriate to grant a sum of Rs.10,000/- under this head. In Rajesh's case (supra), the Apex Court awarded a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- under this head. In the instant case, the accident is of the year 2008 and the deceased was survived by his wife aged 36 years. In the instant case, the mother of the deceased, the fourth respondent/second claimant, was aged 62 years at the time of the accident.
